statement: Persistent disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has reconfigured global fertilizer supply chains: Gulf-origin flows and fertilizer inputs were disrupted, prices surged, import-dependent food systems responded through alternative sourcing, financing, stockpiling and allocation, and by September nitrogen markets had partly adapted while phosphate/sulfur constraints and shipping risk remained.
observed_change: FAO reported on 24 September 2026 that Gulf states supply 30-35% of global urea, about 50% of sulfur exports and 20-30% of ammonia; 1.5-3 million tonnes of monthly fertilizer trade had been delayed and tanker movements through Hormuz had fallen by more than 90%.
World Bank April 2026 commodity analysis recorded the fertilizer price shock, especially urea, and projected elevated 2026 fertilizer prices while noting recovery/adaptation scenarios.
By 21 September, IFPRI/Food Security Portal reported nitrogen markets returning toward pre-war levels while phosphate remained tight and sulfur had emerged as a bottleneck.

Bangladesh received World Bank emergency support for fertilizer imports and continued large procurement/stock allocation; official Bangladesh reporting in August-September stated national stocks were adequate/surplus, preventing an unsupported national-shortage claim.
Australia similarly documented import exposure and intervention, then reported urea arrivals above estimated seasonal demand by August.
why_materially_different_from_benchmark: This is a food-input and trade-resilience shock centered on maritime chokepoints, fertilizer chemistry, import procurement, public finance, crop timing and distribution. It does not depend on AI infrastructure, electricity demand, copper, mining, Chile, or AOC-001's six-Perspective structure.
known_limits: Do not claim a current nationwide fertilizer shortage in Bangladesh or Australia; both documented adequate/surplus supply after intervention.
Do not convert fertilizer price/supply risk directly into observed crop failure or household hunger without location- and period-specific evidence.
Do not treat FAO/World Bank forecasts as observed outcomes.
Do not attribute all fertilizer-market movement to Hormuz; energy costs, export restrictions, production capacity, seasonal demand and other trade disruptions also matter.
Bangladesh is a strong candidate geography, not a preselected story location; geographic resolution must remain evidence-led.
Local farm-level access can diverge from national stock totals and requires separate evidence before asserting local shortage or price effects.
The shock is dynamic: nitrogen adaptation and persistent phosphate/sulfur constraints must be represented rather than frozen at the crisis peak.
